The real story: A 13-metre, roughly 31-tonne humpback whale carcass washed ashore at City Beach in Perth, Western Australia, early on Monday, September 28, 2026. The beach was closed as sharks gathered, a 3.7-metre white shark was tagged and released by the state fisheries department, and contractors removed the carcass to landfill on Wednesday, September 30. Source: ABC News (Australia), published September 28 to 30, 2026.

Surf lifesavers spotted it around 7:30am on Monday, September 28, 2026, a public holiday in Western Australia: a 13-meter humpback whale, estimated at 31 tonnes, lying in the shallows at Perth's City Beach. By the end of the day hundreds of onlookers had come to see it, and the beach had been closed.

Sharks arrived too. Large animals full of blubber are particularly attractive to them, UWA marine biologist Dr. Kate Sprogis explained, which is why the surrounding beaches stayed shut. Western Australia's fisheries department treated the situation as a rare chance for science and tagged and released a 3.7-meter white shark off Floreat Groyne while the carcass was still in the water. Dr. Sprogis also noted that September and October are peak months for humpbacks migrating past the coast, so a death like this isn't unusual for the season.

Then came the part nobody plans for: getting rid of it. Towing a carcass back out to sea depends on conditions, and in this case it went to landfill, with heavy machinery and 6 to 10 workers. The local council estimated the cost at $40,000 to $60,000, with the risk of more if the carcass broke apart. For comparison, a similar job at Scarborough Beach in 2014 cost $188,000, with the state government ending up covering half after a dispute over who should pay. The whale's cause of death has not been reported.

CAN INVISIBLE RADON REVEAL HIDDEN MINERALS? 

Scientists are testing a strange new clue in the deep Pacific.

During a NOAA expedition near American Samoa, researchers are collecting seawater directly above the abyssal seafloor and measuring naturally occurring radon.

Why?

Because radon escaping from sediments could act as a geochemical tracer, potentially helping scientists identify areas where valuable deep-sea minerals may be concentrated.

No drilling.

No giant machines digging through the seafloor.

Just an invisible radioactive gas that may reveal what is hiding below.

🌊 Could the ocean itself be giving scientists clues about what lies underneath?

The real story: A study published September 13, 2026 in the journal Ecology and Evolution, by researchers at the University of the Sunshine Coast, documented a bottlenose dolphin nicknamed Bubbles chasing bigeye trevally at Lady Elliot Island on the southern Great Barrier Reef until they regurgitated, then eating what they brought up. The authors describe it as the first detailed description of kleptoparasitism (food theft) in a cetacean. Source: Smithsonian Magazine, with the University of the Sunshine Coast release via ECO Magazine.

Staff at the Lady Elliot Island Eco Resort, on the southern Great Barrier Reef, nicknamed him Bubbles. Researchers can recognize him from the notches in his fin and a V-shaped scar on his right flank. And between June 2021 and October 2025 they recorded him doing something no one had formally described in a whale or dolphin before.

Bubbles scans a school of bigeye trevally, picks out one fish, and shadows it, mirroring its turns while firing off intense bursts of echolocation clicks and low-pitched sounds. He doesn't try to eat the fish. He keeps chasing it until it throws up its last meal, then swoops in and eats that. Of 20 recorded encounters, 11 ended with Bubbles eating regurgitated food, and he was seen repeating the routine up to 10 times in 30 minutes. Not once was he seen eating the trevally itself.

Why it works is the open question. The researchers suggest the stress of the chase triggers the vomiting, and that echolocation may help Bubbles judge which fish is carrying the fullest stomach; co-author Dr. Asia Haines said the repeated behavior "suggests he may have learnt to target the fish with the fullest bellies." Outside researchers were more cautious about assigning intention, and the team doesn't yet know whether Bubbles invented the trick alone or whether other dolphins do it too. They've asked divers and boaters worldwide to report similar sightings, since this kind of behavior may be happening out of view more often than anyone realizes.

The real story: On Sunday, September 6, 2026, the Samish Indian Nation held a naming ceremony for J63, a female Southern Resident orca born in April 2025 and the first calf of J40, known as Suttles. The tribe's culture committee chose the name Ts'ele7álhse, which means "the heart of the Salish Sea" in Coast Salish. About 100 tribal members attended. Source: KIRO 7 News, published September 17, 2026, with ceremony reporting from the Skagit Valley Herald.

Most Southern Resident orcas get their nicknames from a public vote run by The Whale Museum. The family of J14 is different. For this one orca matriline, the names come from the Samish Indian Nation, whose waters these whales have swum through for thousands of years.

On Sunday, September 6, 2026, about 100 members of the Samish Nation gathered on Samish Island for a naming ceremony during their Camp Samish weekend. The honoree was J63, a female born in April 2025 and the first calf of J40, called Suttles. After much discussion, the tribe's culture committee chose Ts'ele7álhse, "the heart of the Salish Sea." It was the sixth naming for descendants of J2, the famous matriarch Granny. As is tradition, four witnesses were called to record the ceremony and carry the story to others, and a young tribal member, Quinn Burnett, stood in for the calf. Samish elder Leslie Eastwood summed up the feeling in a single line: "We really think of these as our relatives."

The names in this family tell their own story. The matriarch J14 was named Samish, after the nation itself. Her daughter J37 is Hy'Shqa, "blessing." J37's calf J59 is Sxwyeqólh, "Reason for Hope Child." Now the youngest member of J Pod joins that line with a name that places her at the center of the sea her family has traveled for generations. A photograph of Ts'ele7álhse will hang in the Samish council chambers.

The real story: A genetic study led by the Wildlife Conservation Society with the Environment Society of Oman and Oman's Environment Authority, published in Frontiers in Marine Science and reported on September 29, 2026, found that Arabian Sea humpback whales are a distinct, isolated lineage that split from other humpbacks roughly 43,000 to 113,000 years ago. The authors say the result supports recognizing them as a fourth humpback subspecies, proposed as Megaptera novaeangliae indica. Source: Oceanographic Magazine, published September 29, 2026.

Almost every humpback on Earth is a commuter, swimming thousands of kilometers each year between cold feeding grounds and warm breeding waters. The humpbacks of the Arabian Sea never got the memo. They stay in tropical and subtropical water all year, follow a Northern Hemisphere breeding cycle, and sing a song researchers say is heard nowhere else on Earth. They are also the only known humpback population that both feeds and breeds in the same stretch of sea.

On September 29, 2026, a study 25 years in the making put DNA behind what behavior had long hinted at. Comparing the Arabian Sea whales with humpbacks sampled across the species' global range, researchers found a high level of genetic difference from the three recognized subspecies of the North Atlantic, North Pacific and Southern Hemisphere, and the lowest genetic diversity of any ocean region examined. Ancient DNA from the 1883 type specimen, a whale collected near Basra, Iraq and now held in Paris, was a close match to today's population. Lead author Dr. Rita Amaral said these whales "have long been an enigma." The formal call on a new subspecies belongs to the Society for Marine Mammalogy's Taxonomy Committee.

The finding comes with a warning attached. The population is small, with no sign of growth in two decades, and faces entanglement, ship strikes, noise, pollution and disease, while shifting monsoons may change how much sardine prey is available. The International Whaling Commission has already recognized the group as a discrete population and recommended a Conservation Management Plan. If the study is right, this is a lineage that has gone its own way for tens of thousands of years, and one that could disappear without ever being widely known.

The real story: A young Bigg's killer whale known as T65B2 stranded near Minor Island, British Columbia, on July 16, 2026, and remained on the beach for at least five hours before successfully refloating and rejoining his family group by late afternoon. Source: Orca Behavior Institute, published July 2026.

On July 16, 2026, a young Bigg's killer whale from the T65B pod, known to researchers as T65B2, ended up stranded near Minor Island off the coast of British Columbia. For any orca, being stuck out of the water is a genuine emergency — their massive bodies aren't built to support their own weight on land, and prolonged stranding can cause serious, sometimes fatal, internal damage.

He stayed grounded for at least five hours. What happened next is the detail that makes this story worth telling: rather than moving on, his family group stayed close by or returned to the area, and by late afternoon, T65B2 had successfully refloated himself and rejoined them. Researchers who track Bigg's killer whale families closely say this kind of outcome — a young whale stranding and getting back to open water under its own power, with family nearby — is genuinely uncommon, and reflects both the tidal luck of the moment and the tight social bonds that define orca pods.

For a family group whose comings and goings are tracked in detail by researchers up and down the Pacific coast, this was a close call that resolved itself in an afternoon — and one more data point in just how much orca survival can come down to who's around when things go wrong.

The real story: A young humpback whale found entangled in heavy coaxial cable off Maui in 2017 was freed by NOAA's Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary team. In 2024, a member of the public uploaded a photo of a whale's fluke to the citizen-science platform HappyWhale, and researchers confirmed it was the same whale — now a healthy adult with no visible injuries. Source: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, published 2025.

In 2017, a young humpback whale off the coast of Maui was found anchored in place by hundreds of feet of heavy coaxial cable, struggling to breathe. Responders from NOAA's Hawaiian Islands Humpback Whale National Marine Sanctuary managed to free her — but as with most entanglement rescues, the team had no way of knowing whether she'd actually survive long-term. Once a freed whale swims away, it usually disappears from the record for good.

Seven years later, in 2024, that changed. A member of the public on a Maui boat trip photographed a whale's tail fluke and uploaded it to HappyWhale.com, a global platform that lets anyone match individual whales by the unique markings on their flukes. Sanctuary researchers ran the image against their records and got the confirmation they'd been hoping for without ever expecting to actually receive it: it was the same whale. Now a fully grown adult, she showed no remaining gear, no visible scarring, and no signs of injury at all — remarkably close to where responders had freed her nearly a decade earlier.

Since 2022 alone, Hawai'i's whale entanglement network has freed 44 large whales and removed more than 15,690 feet of line and netting from the region's waters. Most of those stories end the same way this one almost did: with a whale swimming off into open ocean and researchers left to hope for the best. This time, a stranger's vacation photo turned that hope into an actual answer.

The real story: Researchers spotted at least eight Bryde's whales off Weizhou Island in China's Beibu Gulf on September 24, 2026, including two mothers with calves — the pod's first sighting there since April, and the eighth consecutive year they've returned before the Mid-Autumn Festival. The Weizhou population, estimated at roughly 60 individuals, is the largest known resident group of the species in Chinese waters. Source: Xinhua, published September 24, 2026.

Weizhou Island sits in China's Beibu Gulf, a volcanic island most famous for its rocky reefs and diving tourism. It's also home to something far rarer: the only stable population of resident whales anywhere in Chinese coastal waters, a group of roughly 60 Bryde's whales that researchers have been tracking since a resident first sent in a shaky video clip back in 2016.

On September 24, 2026, researchers spotted at least eight of them together, including two mothers swimming with calves — their first confirmed sighting in the area since April. What makes the timing genuinely striking is that this wasn't a one-off: it's the eighth year running that the whales have shown up right before China's Mid-Autumn Festival, the holiday built entirely around family reunions. Long-term photo-identification work has found some of these whales show remarkable site fidelity, with individual animals documented returning to the same small patch of ocean across multiple survey periods spanning years.

Scientists studying the population have used everything from boat-based photo surveys to an onshore seismometer on nearby Xieyang Island to listen for the whales' low-frequency calls, building one of the most detailed pictures of coastal Bryde's whale behavior anywhere in the world. Researchers have also proposed a marine protected zone within 20 kilometers of Weizhou Island, citing evidence that vessel traffic and nighttime lighting may already be affecting where the whales choose to feed.

The real story: A study analyzing 199 distinct feeding observations from social media and citizen-science footage, representing an estimated 1,417 individual humpback whales feeding in Australian waters between 2013 and 2024, challenges the long-held "feast or famine" assumption that humpbacks fast throughout their migration. Source: Australian Geographic, published August 2026.

For decades, the textbook story about humpback whale migration went like this: whales gorge themselves on krill in Antarctic waters, then essentially stop eating for months as they migrate thousands of kilometers north to breed in warm tropical waters, running purely on stored fat until they return south again. It's a tidy story. A new study suggests it's also wrong, at least for a lot of whales.

Since conducting large-scale survey research across thousands of kilometers of coastline isn't financially realistic, researchers took a different approach: they combed through public posts from whale-watching companies, drone pilots, and dedicated whale enthusiasts on platforms like Facebook and Instagram, searching for clear visual evidence of feeding behavior — mouths open, expanded ventral pleats, bubble-net formations, or whales surfacing directly through dense schools of baitfish. Only posts with unambiguous visual proof made the cut.

The final tally: 199 distinct feeding events, representing an estimated 1,417 individual humpback whales documented actively feeding in Australian waters between 2013 and 2024 — a migration route where, according to the old model, they shouldn't have been eating much at all. Rather than a strict feast-or-famine pattern, the data suggests many humpbacks are opportunistically feeding throughout their journey whenever the chance presents itself, quietly rewriting one of the most repeated facts about one of the ocean's most-studied animals.

The real story: A Georgia Department of Natural Resources team spent two days in December 2025 partially disentangling a four-year-old North Atlantic right whale nicknamed "Division" (#5217) off the Georgia coast. He was later found showing declining health via satellite tag, and NOAA determined in April 2026 that rope recovered from him was consistent with gear used in Canada's Snow Crab Fishing Area 12 in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence. Source: The Current (Georgia), published December 6, 2025, and NOAA Fisheries North Atlantic Right Whale Health Updates, April 2026.

He was born to a right whale named Silt and known for most of his life only as catalog number 5217 — until the markings on his head, resembling a mathematical division symbol, earned him a name. In December 2025, a Georgia Department of Natural Resources team led by biologist Clay George spent two exhausting days trying to save him.

The team's 26-foot boat, the RV Timucua, reached Division off the Georgia coast with commercial fishing gear wrapped around his massive body. Day one was about tracking and preparation: the team attached a satellite tag to the trailing rope — thick as a garden hose — so they could find him again the next day without increasing the immediate risk to the whale. Over the following two days, working with aerial survey teams and partner agencies, they managed to remove a significant portion of the entangling gear, a painstaking, dangerous process carried out from a small boat beside an animal the size of a bus.

It wasn't enough. Telemetry later showed Division moving north into New England waters, then drifting back south with a pattern researchers recognized as decline rather than travel. Poor weather and his distance from shore made further disentanglement impossible, and by January 2026, his satellite track suggested he was no longer swimming under his own power. In April, NOAA Fisheries and Fisheries and Oceans Canada finished analyzing the rope the team had managed to recover months earlier: the markings matched gear used in Canada's Snow Crab Fishing Area 12, in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence — a definitive answer to where his entanglement began, arriving long after there was anything left to do with it.

The real story: Researchers at NOAA's Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary, led by research ecologist David Wiley, attached video-camera tags to wild humpback whales and recorded 110 seafloor hunting events in which whales approached each other to form a "star" formation — rostrums pointed toward a shared central point — to corral sand lance before feeding together. It's the first time collaborative seafloor hunting has been directly documented in humpback whales. The study was published in Behavioural Ecology and Sociobiology. Source: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, and Discover Wildlife (BBC Wildlife), published August 6, 2026.

Everyone pictures humpback whales feeding at the surface — mouths open, bursting through the water in a spray of foam. Scientists at NOAA's Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary just filmed something almost nobody had seen: what humpbacks do when they hunt down on the seafloor itself.

Using tags fitted with video cameras and attached directly to wild whales, the research team captured 110 separate seafloor hunting events in the Gulf of Maine. What they noticed was a strikingly deliberate pattern: whales swimming along the bottom would approach each other and arrange themselves into what the researchers called a "star" formation, their rostrums all pointed toward one shared central point, sometimes just a few meters apart, sometimes almost touching. "In events with at least two animals, they moved toward each other to form a 'star' formation, with rostrums pointed to a central location among the whales," the study's authors wrote. Working together this way helped the whales corral their prey — tiny fish called sand lance — into a tight group before opening their mouths at nearly the same instant to feed.

"We do not yet know whether this collaborative strategy is unique to humpback whales hunting sand lance in the Gulf of Maine or if it occurs in other whale populations and habitats," said lead author David Wiley, the sanctuary's research ecologist. The discovery comes with a worrying footnote: because this behavior happens right along the seafloor, it puts the whales at significantly higher risk of becoming tangled in bottom-set fishing gear — the exact kind of entanglement responders spend all year trying to prevent.

The real story: Osiris, a 26-year-old female beluga rescued from the closed Marineland park in Ontario, died at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium on September 22, 2026 — the third rescued beluga to die at Shedd, following Peekachu (Aug 26) and Rain (Sept 2). A fourth whale, Jelly Bean, died the same week at Oceanogràfic Valencia in Spain. Source: Associated Press, published September 22, 2026.

Osiris arrived at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium in mid-July 2026, one of the first four beluga whales rescued from Marineland, a shuttered marine park in Niagara Falls, Ontario, whose caretakers had threatened to euthanize the animals if new homes couldn't be found. At 26 years old, she wasn't the easiest eater at first. But with fluids, medication, and care, her appetite improved, and staff say her "commanding personality" began to emerge as she engaged with the other rescued whales.

On Monday morning, September 22, aquarium staff noticed changes in her behavior and breathing. Her condition declined quickly, and despite lifesaving efforts, she died. "Though Osiris was with us for far less time than we had hoped, her care was never measured by its length," Shedd wrote in a blog post. She's the third rescued whale to die at Shedd this month, after 23-year-old Peekachu on August 26 and 20-year-old Rain on September 2 — and the same week Shedd announced Osiris's death, a fourth rescued whale, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanogràfic Valencia in Spain, one of the international facilities that also took in animals from the closed park.

"Four animals have died so shortly after arriving in the new homes, and that's what stands out to me as being surprising," said marine mammal researcher Andrew Trites. Shedd, which took in 10 of the more than two dozen relocated whales, says the cause of Osiris's death is still unknown and a necropsy is underway; results from the earlier deaths remain pending too. "That uncertainty does not lessen the heartbreak of Osiris's loss," the aquarium wrote, "or our responsibility to examine it with scientific rigor and open-hearted transparency."

The real story: Three dolphins — two young bottlenose dolphins and one adult common dolphin — washed ashore within a two-week span in Nelson Mandela Bay, South Africa, in September 2026. Marine mammal expert Dr. Greg Hofmeyr said there was no clear cause of death yet and urged the public not to be alarmed. Source: Daily Maverick, published September 17, 2026.

In the span of about two weeks in September 2026, three dolphins washed up along the same stretch of coastline in Nelson Mandela Bay, South Africa — enough of a pattern that local residents started asking whether something was seriously wrong in the water.

The most recent, an adult common dolphin, was found at Denville Beach on September 15, still fresh, with no obvious signs of what killed it. Days earlier, two young bottlenose dolphins had washed up nearby at King's Beach — one recently deceased, the other already badly decomposed, suggesting it had died at sea days before drifting ashore. Marine mammal expert Dr. Greg Hofmeyr, who has been examining the animals, said it wasn't yet clear whether the most recent dolphin was already dead before it reached the beach, or died shortly after stranding, and that it showed no obvious external cause of death.

Multiple unrelated strandings in a short window can look alarming from the outside, but marine biologists caution that it doesn't automatically point to a single underlying crisis — dolphins strand for a wide range of individual reasons, from illness to injury to simply being at the end of a natural lifespan, and three unconnected deaths in two weeks isn't necessarily unusual for a busy stretch of coastline. Experts say the real answer will only come once necropsy results are in — until then, the message from researchers is to keep watching, not to jump to conclusions.

The real story: An international research team, including scientists from Aarhus University, measured "slow clicks" produced by large male sperm whales off Seychelles, Sri Lanka, Norway, and Scotland, finding them to be the highest-source-level communication sounds ever recorded from a mammal — distinct from the whales' echolocation clicks, and capable of traveling up to 70 kilometers underwater. The study was published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2026. Source: phys.org, published August 3, 2026.

Sperm whales are already known for using some of the most powerful sounds in the ocean to find food — rapid clicks that bounce off prey hundreds of meters below the surface. But an international team of researchers just confirmed that male sperm whales make a completely different kind of sound, one purely for talking to each other, and it's louder than anything else ever measured coming out of a mammal.

Working with recordings gathered off Seychelles, Sri Lanka, Norway, and Scotland, the team — including researchers from Aarhus University's Center for Active Sensing with Sound — identified slow, rhythmic clicks made specifically by large adult males, distinct in structure and purpose from the fast clicks whales use for echolocation. These "slow clicks" carry the highest source levels of any known mammalian communication signal, loud enough to potentially travel up to 70 kilometers through favorable ocean conditions before fading out.

What the sound is actually for is still unresolved. Researchers suspect it may function as a way for males to advertise their size or compete for attention across enormous distances, though the behavioral purpose remains unconfirmed. There's also a modern complication: the researchers noted that shipping noise, now a near-constant presence in much of the ocean, can significantly cut down how far these signals actually travel — meaning the loudest voice in the mammal kingdom may be getting harder for other whales to hear.

The real story: A study published in Royal Society Open Science in May 2026 by researchers at Griffith University confirmed two individual humpback whales traveled between breeding grounds in eastern Australia and Brazil, using photo-matching of over 19,000 tail-fluke images collected over four decades. One whale's confirmed distance between sightings — 15,100 kilometers — set a new record for the longest documented movement of an individual humpback whale. Source: ScienceDaily/Griffith University, published May 19, 2026.

Humpback whales are famous for long migrations, but they're not famous for switching oceans entirely. That's exactly what researchers just confirmed two individual whales did — connecting breeding populations that were never known to mix.

Using an automated image-recognition program to sift through more than 19,000 tail-fluke photographs collected over four decades, scientists at Griffith University, working with researchers in Brazil and the United States, matched two whales photographed on opposite sides of the planet. One was first photographed off Bahia, Brazil, in 2003, at the Abrolhos Bank — the country's main humpback nursery. Twenty-two years later, in September 2025, the same whale turned up alone in Hervey Bay, Australia, more than 15,100 kilometers away — the longest confirmed distance ever recorded between sightings of a single humpback whale anywhere on Earth. A second whale made the reverse trip: first seen in Hervey Bay in 2007, then off São Paulo, Brazil, in 2019, a straight-line distance of roughly 14,200 kilometers, comparable to flying from Sydney to London.

Because only the start and end points of each journey were documented, researchers don't actually know the route either whale took, or how much farther they may have traveled to get there. What makes the discovery even more striking is just how rare it appears to be: across more than 40 years of data covering nearly 20,000 individually identified humpback whales, these are the only two ever found to have crossed between the Australian and Brazilian breeding populations — just 0.01% of the entire record. Rare as they are, scientists say these outlier journeys could matter far more than their numbers suggest, potentially carrying genetic diversity between populations that would otherwise never mix at all.

The real story: The 2025–2026 North Atlantic right whale calving season produced at least 23 documented calves — the highest number since 2009 — according to aerial and boat survey teams working off Florida and Georgia. Source: The Current (Georgia), published April 21, 2026.

North Atlantic right whales migrate to the warm coastal waters off Georgia and Florida every winter for one reason: to give birth. With fewer than 400 of these whales left on Earth, survey teams treat every single calf sighting as a data point that matters. This past winter, they counted at least 23 of them — the most in almost two decades.

Aerial and boat survey crews began documenting mother-calf pairs in December 2025 and kept counting through the season's final weeks. By the time it wrapped up, the total reached at least 23 confirmed calves, the highest count since 2009 — a genuinely dramatic swing for a species that, in some recent years, has produced barely a handful. Researchers had set a rough benchmark for what counts as a "successful" season: around 20 calves. This year cleared that bar.

Scientists remain careful not to call it a turning point. North Atlantic right whales need an estimated 50 new calves a year just to grow the population back toward stability, and the species remains caught in what NOAA calls an ongoing "Unusual Mortality Event," with roughly 20% of the population sick, injured, or killed by vessel strikes and entanglement since 2017. Twenty-three calves in a single season doesn't undo that. But for a species whose headlines are almost always about loss, it's the rare kind of number researchers were genuinely happy to report.
